conversation.content: Let's design a real-time chat system like Slack or WhatsApp. It needs to support 1-on-1 messaging and group chats. What questions do you have?
I think... maybe the first thing to understand is the scale? How many users, and how many concurrent connections are we expecting? And I guess group sizes matter too?
100 million total users, 10 million concurrent at peak. Groups up to 100,000 members. Average message size 1KB. What's your initial thinking on the high-level architecture?
I think... maybe WebSocket? For the real-time part? Since we need messages delivered instantly, HTTP polling would be too slow. So clients would maintain a persistent connection to our servers.
WebSocket is a good choice. Why WebSocket over something like Server-Sent Events or long polling?

Well, WebSocket is full-duplex — both the client and server can send data at any time. SSE is server-to-client only, so we'd still need a separate HTTP channel for sending messages. Long polling has higher latency and more overhead from constantly re-establishing connections. For a chat system where both sides need to send and receive, WebSocket is the natural fit. I'm more confident about this choice now that I think through the alternatives.
Good reasoning. Now 10 million concurrent WebSocket connections — how do you handle that?

A single server can handle maybe 50,000 to 100,000 concurrent WebSocket connections — it's mainly limited by memory for connection state. So we need at least 100 to 200 servers for the connection layer. Let me call these Connection Gateway servers. They're stateful — each one knows which users are connected to it. We need a way to route a message from one user to the gateway holding the recipient's connection. I think we need a mapping service — something like Redis — that tracks which user is on which gateway.
You're on the right track. Walk me through the full message flow — User A sends a message to User B.

Okay. User A's client sends the message over their WebSocket to Gateway 1. Gateway 1 forwards it to a Message Service, which writes it to the message store for durability. The Message Service then looks up which gateway User B is connected to via the presence service backed by Redis. Say User B is on Gateway 5. The Message Service publishes the message to Gateway 5, which pushes it down User B's WebSocket. If User B is offline, the message stays in the store and is delivered when B reconnects and pulls unread messages. Actually, I realize the Message Service shouldn't directly call Gateway 5 — that creates tight coupling. Better to use a pub/sub layer. Each gateway subscribes to channels for all its connected users. The Message Service publishes to the recipient's channel.
Good self-correction on the pub/sub. What pub/sub system would you use?

For 10 million concurrent users, we need a pub/sub system that handles millions of channels efficiently. Redis Pub/Sub is lightweight but doesn't persist messages and has single-node limitations. Kafka persists messages but isn't designed for millions of topics — one per user would be excessive. I'd use a purpose-built system. Actually, for this use case, I'd have the gateways use consistent hashing to route messages. Each gateway is responsible for delivering to a deterministic subset of users. The Message Service uses the same hash function to know which gateway to send to. This avoids the pub/sub bottleneck entirely — it's direct routing with the hash providing the mapping without a centralized lookup.
Interesting approach. But if you use consistent hashing, doesn't the user need to connect to a specific gateway? What happens to load balancing?

Right, there's a tension. We need a connection gateway with consistent hashing, here's why and how to balance it: The initial WebSocket connection goes through a regular L4 load balancer. But we add a routing layer. When a user connects to any gateway, that gateway registers the user-to-gateway mapping in a lightweight presence service — a distributed hash table or Redis Cluster. When a message arrives for delivery, the Message Service looks up the recipient's gateway from the presence service and routes directly. This gives us the best of both worlds: load balancing for connections (users connect anywhere) and direct routing for messages (no broadcast). The consistent hashing idea was wrong — it forces sticky sessions that break during scaling events. The presence service is the right abstraction.
Now you're thinking clearly. Let's talk about message storage. How do you store messages for a system at this scale?

Messages are append-heavy with reads typically being sequential scans of recent history. This is perfect for a write-optimized store. I'd use Cassandra with the partition key as conversation_id and clustering key as message_timestamp. This means all messages in a conversation are co-located on the same partition, and reading the latest N messages is a single sequential scan. For sizing: if we have 50 million messages per day at 1KB each, that's 50GB per day, 18TB per year. With a replication factor of 3, that's 54TB per year — a modest Cassandra cluster handles this easily. For older messages, we can tier to cheaper storage — messages older than 1 year go to S3, loaded on demand.
How do you handle group chats with 100,000 members? That's the hard part.

100K-member groups are essentially a broadcast problem. We absolutely cannot do a point-to-point delivery to each member — looking up 100K gateways and sending 100K individual messages per chat message is too slow. Here's my approach: a Group Delivery Service that maintains a mapping of group_id to the set of gateways that have at least one connected member. When a message is sent to the group, the service sends one copy to each relevant gateway — say 150 gateways — not 100K individual deliveries. Each gateway then locally fans out to its connected members of that group. This is a two-level fan-out: service-to-gateways, then gateway-to-connections. The gateway maintains an in-memory index of group_id to local connections for fast local fan-out. For offline members, we don't store individual copies — we store the message once in Cassandra and each member fetches their unread messages on reconnect by querying the conversation's message history since their last-read timestamp.
Excellent. How do you guarantee message ordering in this system?

Message ordering is subtle in a distributed system. We can't rely on wall clock time because servers have clock skew. I'd use a hybrid approach: each message gets a server-assigned timestamp from the Message Service, but within a conversation, we use a monotonically increasing sequence number. The sequence number is generated per-conversation — a simple atomic increment in Redis keyed by conversation_id. This guarantees total ordering within a conversation. For display, we order by sequence number, not timestamp. In rare cases where two messages arrive at the Message Service simultaneously, the one that gets the lower sequence number displays first. The client maintains a local buffer and orders by sequence number, requesting gap-fills if it detects a missing sequence number.
What about read receipts and typing indicators? Those are real-time features that generate a lot of traffic.

These are ephemeral signals — they don't need persistence. Typing indicators are fire-and-forget: send over WebSocket to the gateway, which routes to the other participants' gateways. No database write, no queue. If it's lost, the worst case is a missed typing indicator — tolerable. For read receipts, they need a bit more reliability. When User A reads a message, we update a last_read pointer in a lightweight store — Redis with the key conversation:{id}:user:{id}:last_read. This is sent to other participants for the 'seen' indicator. In large groups, we aggregate — instead of showing 'seen by 50,000 people,' we show 'seen by User X, User Y, and 49,998 others' and only track the detailed breakdown lazily. The key insight is to not treat these the same as messages — different reliability guarantees, different storage, different delivery paths.
What happens when a gateway server goes down? How do clients recover?

When a gateway dies, all its connections drop. The client detects the broken WebSocket and reconnects through the load balancer to a new gateway. On reconnect, the client sends its last-seen sequence number per conversation. The new gateway fetches all messages with higher sequence numbers from Cassandra and delivers them. The presence service detects the gateway failure via heartbeat timeout and cleans up stale entries. During the reconnection window — typically 1-5 seconds — incoming messages for those users are handled by the Message Service's retry logic: if delivery to a gateway fails, the message stays in the queue and is retried. Once the user reconnects and their new gateway registers with the presence service, pending messages are delivered. No messages are lost because the source of truth is Cassandra, not the gateway.
We're almost out of time. Any final considerations?

A few important production concerns. End-to-end encryption for 1-on-1 chats using a protocol like Signal — the server never sees plaintext. Push notifications via APNs and FCM for offline users — a separate notification service that checks the presence service before sending, to avoid redundant pushes to online users. Message search using an inverted index — Elasticsearch, partitioned by user_id so searches are scoped. File and media sharing through a separate upload service with CDN distribution. And rate limiting per user to prevent spam, especially in large groups. Looking back at this interview, I'm glad I worked through the routing problem thoroughly — the presence service approach is much cleaner than my initial consistent hashing idea, and it enabled the two-level fan-out for groups naturally.
Your confidence really grew throughout this interview. The depth on group delivery, ordering, and failure handling was impressive. Thank you.

strengths: Remarkable confidence growth — from hesitant one-line answers to commanding technical explanations
Excellent two-level fan-out design for large group message delivery
Thoughtful differentiation of reliability tiers for messages vs ephemeral signals
weaknesses: Weak start with hesitant communication undermined first impression
Requirements gathering was minimal — didn't ask about message history, search, or compliance
Initial routing design needed course correction from consistent hashing to presence service
